options: Only data stored in the database
Data permanently, even after the API processes it
Only the URL, not the body
Data while it travels from consumer to API; it is decrypted at the API
quiz.explain: HTTPS encrypts data in transit so an interceptor sees gibberish; once it reaches the API it is decrypted and processed normally.

quiz.q: Employee 102 exists. You send all of 102's details with a new email and phone, replacing the whole record. Which method fits?
quiz.explain: PUT replaces the entire resource (or creates it if it doesn't exist). PATCH would update only specific fields.

quiz.q: You need to change only employee 102's phone number, leaving all other fields untouched. Which method is the standard choice?
quiz.explain: PATCH is a partial update; PUT replaces the whole resource.

quiz.q: What is the difference between POST and PUT according to the lecture?
options: POST fetches data; PUT creates data
POST creates a new resource (error if it exists, by design); PUT replaces it if it exists or creates it if not
quiz.explain: PUT is also idempotent — sending the same PUT twice gives the same result — while POST is not.

quiz.q: As a standard, how should a GET request pass the employee ID?
options: Through query or URI parameters, not a body
quiz.explain: GET should not carry a body; use `?employeeId=123` (query) or `/employees/123` (URI parameter).
Query parameters start with `?` and are `key=value` pairs separated by `&`, typically for filtering, sorting or pagination.

quiz.q: What do headers carry in an HTTP request?
options: The main message of the request
Metadata — data about data, e.g. Content-Type or source system
quiz.explain: The body carries the main message; headers carry metadata like `Content-Type: application/json` or `source: mobile-application`.

quiz.q: A consumer sends correct credentials but calls a resource they have no access to. Which status code fits?
quiz.explain: 401 means credentials are missing or wrong; 403 means authenticated but not permitted for that resource.

quiz.q: The API accepts only JSON but the client sends an XML body. Which status code should be returned?
quiz.explain: 415 is for an unsupported body format; 405 is for a wrong HTTP method.

quiz.q: A client sends a correct request, but the API's database is down. Which series of status code applies?
quiz.explain: The client did nothing wrong; the problem is on the API side, so a 5xx (e.g. 500) is returned.

quiz.q: By the HTTP standard, a gateway that doesn't receive a timely response from the upstream API returns which code?
quiz.explain: 504 = no timely response; 502 = the gateway received an invalid response (or couldn't connect).

quiz.q: In JSON, what is the type of the value in `"resigned": "true"`?
quiz.explain: Booleans are written without quotes (`true`/`false`). A quoted `"true"` is a string.

cards.back: HyperText Transfer Protocol — used to structure and transfer requests and responses over the internet; data travels as readable plain text.
HTTP Secure — encrypts data **in transit** with a key and algorithm. Decrypted at the API. In Mule it's the same HTTP connector with TLS configuration.
GET fetch · POST create · PUT replace fully (or create if absent) · PATCH partial update · DELETE remove.
POST creates a new resource (by design, error if it exists). PUT replaces if it exists or creates if not; PUT is idempotent.
PUT replaces the entire resource; PATCH changes only the fields sent.
Only if the API is designed to restrict them. They're standards — like traffic rules — follow them so everyone understands.
`protocol://host:port/resource-path`, e.g. `http://localhost:8081/empdetails`. All parts must match the Listener.
Protocol, host, port, resource path (URL), method, query/URI parameters, headers, authorization, body.
Body = the main message (JSON, XML, text). Headers = metadata, "data about data" (Content-Type, source system).
`?key=value&key2=value2` at the end of the URL — used to filter, sort or paginate.
Part of the path that uniquely identifies a resource, e.g. `/employees/{empid}` → `/employees/100`.

cards.front: Who decides which request parts are mandatory?
cards.back: The API owner, at **design** time: methods, body fields, headers, query params, security.
1xx informational · 2xx success · 3xx redirection · 4xx client error · 5xx server error. 1xx/3xx are rare in APIs.
200 OK — data returned · 201 Created — new resource created · 204 No Content — success, nothing to return.
Request malformed or invalid — e.g. a mandatory field missing or salary sent as text `"80000"` instead of a number.
401: credentials missing or wrong. 403: credentials valid, but not allowed to access that resource.
404 resource not found (e.g. `/empdetails1`) · 405 method not allowed · 415 unsupported media type (body format).
500 internal server error (e.g. DB down) · 501 functionality not implemented · 503 service unavailable.
502 Bad Gateway: gateway got an invalid response (or couldn't connect). 504 Gateway Timeout: no timely response from upstream.
Component in front of the API — like a security guard — that checks credentials and forwards valid requests.
JavaScript Object Notation — simple text format. Object = `{ }`, array = `[ ]`; keys in double quotes; key and value separated by `:`, properties by `,`.
String, number, boolean, null, object, array. `true`/`false`/`null` are unquoted. **No date type** — dates are strings.
One key with `[...]` handles any number of values of the same kind, instead of `hobby1`, `hobby2`, `hobby3`.
